tldr: The authors introduce RFW-W, a physical asset universe containing over one million simulation-ready assets spanning rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Using its rigid asset collection, RFW-R—equipped with physical properties and grasp annotations—they demonstrate scene fulfillment rates and robot manipulation policy learning performance that substantially outperform existing methods.
hero_caption: An overall view of RFW-W. Three distinct asset sources—deformables on the left (RFW-S), rigids in the center (RFW-R), and articulated objects on the right (RFW-A)—are unified through a common interface, enabling the automated construction of task-conditioned embodied simulation environments.
overview:
For robots to perform diverse tasks in the real world, training them in large and diverse simulated environments is key. However, existing 3D models and meshes from generative models found on the web, while visually appealing, lack critical physical information—such as mass, friction, collision geometry, and joint structures—needed for robots to physically interact with and manipulate them. This causes physics engines to fail and limits the scaling of simulation-based training.

To overcome this, the authors propose RFW-W (RoboFlywheel-World), an ultra-large-scale physical asset universe unifying rigid, articulated (such as doors and drawers), and deformable (such as cloth and soft bodies) objects. In total, it comprises 1,010,386 asset records across 2,228 categories. This paper focuses in particular on the construction pipeline and validation of its core rigid collection, RFW-R, which contains over 520,000 assets. In RFW-R, everything is end-to-end automated: shape generation via generative AI, multi-view quality inspection using vision-language models (VLMs), functional part segmentation, collision geometry generation via convex decomposition, part-level physical property estimation, and grasp simulation verification across six types of robotic hands.

Validation experiments thoroughly evaluated behavioral consistency across multiple physics simulators, dexterous hand grasping success rates, instruction-conditioned room scene composition capabilities, and manipulation policy learning via imitation learning. As a result, policies trained on RFW-R data surpassed major existing datasets (such as ManiTwin) by over 10 to 15 percentage points in success rates, and the generated simulation trajectories were shown to be directly replayable on real robots.
contributions: Constructed RFW-W, a physical simulation-ready asset universe of over 1 million assets across 2,228 categories, comprising rigid (520k), articulated (400k), and deformable (80k) objects.

Established an automated pipeline for rigid assets (RFW-R) covering generation, multi-view VLM quality assurance, part-level physical property estimation, and grasp verification with 6 multi-fingered hands.
Quantitatively demonstrated high behavioral consistency (80.77%) in free-fall drop tests for identical assets across four major simulators: PyBullet, MuJoCo, Genesis, and Isaac Sim.

Achieved 100% fulfillment in instruction-conditioned task-driven scene composition and demonstrated over a 10 percentage point improvement in policy learning success rates over the strongest baseline.

sections.heading: Why Robot Learning Demands Physical Assets, Not Just Visuals
sections.summary: Generalizing embodied robotic intelligence requires training across diverse environments, but conventional 3D datasets are appearance-centric and lack the information needed for physical simulation. This paper introduces RFW-W, a million-scale foundation spanning rigid, articulated, and deformable objects with executable physical representations.
sections.details:
Because collecting real-world data involves immense costs and safety risks, large-scale data generation via physical simulation has become the primary battleground for robot learning. However, the true bottleneck of any simulator lies in the quality and quantity of the 3D assets (object models) it runs.

Modern 3D repositories and generative models can produce millions of meshes, but most are merely "hollow shells." Running realistic simulations demands real-world scale, collision geometry (colliders), mass, friction, moments of inertia, and interaction information specifying where and how a robot can grasp an object. While existing physical datasets like YCB and Google Scanned Objects offer high quality, they are small—ranging from a few dozen to around a thousand objects—and lack category diversity.

RFW-W was introduced to break through this barrier. It boasts an unprecedented scale: 524,611 rigid assets (RFW-R), 402,410 articulated assets (RFW-A), and 83,365 deformable assets (RFW-S). Designed to support task-conditioned asset retrieval and scene composition via a common interface, this study thoroughly validates the quality, cross-simulator reproducibility, and robot learning effectiveness of the rigid pipeline, RFW-R.

sections.heading: From 3D Asset Generation to Simulating the Physical World
sections.summary: Focus has shifted from collecting and generating visual CG models to researching assets endowed with physical properties and articulated parts. This work addresses the small category scales and lack of part-level physical representations in prior work, serving as an upstream, unified asset foundation.
sections.details:
### 3D Asset Collection and the Evolution of Physical Datasets
With the emergence of repositories like Objaverse, visual 3D meshes have exploded, and generative models such as TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D have enabled open-category 3D generation. However, these focus on visual shape reconstruction and are not built for simulation. In response, efforts such as ManiTwin, Seed3D, and EmbodiedGen have begun adding physical properties and grasp annotations, yet their covered categories and asset counts remain limited, and support for dexterous multi-fingered manipulation has been insufficient.

### Physicalization and Interaction Representations
"Physicalization"—making shapes operable inside a simulator—requires identifying functional parts and creating suitable collision geometry. Prior studies have proposed convex decomposition via CoACD as well as volume and mass estimation via PUGS. RFW-R builds upon these by integrating semantic part-level material and friction estimation, volume-based inertia tensor synthesis, and grasp annotation generation through contact, lifting, and perturbation tests across multiple robot hand types into a single pipeline.

### Scene Generation and Robot Policies
Research on automatically generating entire indoor scenes from prompts (such as Infinigen) and learning policies from large-scale data (such as Diffusion Policy and Open X-Embodiment) is advancing rapidly. RFW-W provides a unified retrieval interface serving as an "upstream physical foundation" that supports downstream scene composition and data collection.

sections.heading: The Architecture Powering Generation, Physicalization, and Scene Composition for a Million Assets
sections.summary: RFW-W comprises three streams—rigid, articulated, and deformable assets—integrated through a unified interface. Its core rigid pipeline, RFW-R, automatically handles generation, VLM quality assurance, part segmentation, collision modeling, physical property estimation, and grasp verification to enable instruction-conditioned scene composition.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Three Major Physical Asset Sources and the Common Interface
RFW-W integrates three asset sources:
- **RFW-R (Rigid)**: Over 520,000 assets across 1,212 categories. The primary focus of this paper, handling everything from generation to simulation verification end-to-end.
- **RFW-A (Articulated)**: Over 400,000 assets across 531 categories. Uses reusable procedural generator scripts to explicitly preserve joint structures and link hierarchies for doors, drawers, and more.
- **RFW-S (Deformable)**: Over 80,000 assets across 485 categories. Supports PBD (Position-Based Dynamics) and MPM (Material Point Method), with verified physical responses and runtime overheads for garments, bags, and soft bodies.
These are abstracted through a common interface, enabling task-conditioned retrieval.

### 3.2 Category-Guided Rigid Generation Pipeline (L0–L2)
RFW-R is built through a staged automated pipeline (L0–L5). First, at L0, Qwen3.7-plus generates diverse object prompts, FLUX.2-klein converts them into images, and TRELLIS.2 reconstructs them into 3D meshes. At L1, the mesh is rendered from five canonical views (front, back, left, right, bottom), and at L2, a VLM (Qwen3.7-plus) inspects whether it is a "single object," "suitable as a rigid body," and "free of geometric defects." Category misclassifications are routed through a relabeling and re-inspection loop to minimize unnecessary discards.

### 3.3 Physicalization and Multi-Fingered Grasp Annotation (L3–L4)
Meshes that pass visual QA are segmented into parts using P3-SAM at L3 and decomposed into multiple convex hulls using CoACD to preserve concavities. At L4, a VLM estimates part-level material, density, friction coefficient, and real-world scale. Part mass $m_p = \rho_p V_p$ is calculated from part volume $V_p$ and density $\rho_p$, and the overall center of mass and inertia tensor are synthesized using the parallel axis theorem. If the ratio relative to the holistic estimated mass falls outside $[0.5, 2]$, joint scaling is applied for consistency. Furthermore, using an extension of TRO-Grasp across six robotic hand types, grasp poses are simulated (evaluating contact, penetration, grasping, lifting, and perturbation robustness), recording only executable poses. Final assets are exported to URDF, MJCF, and USD formats.

### 3.4 Task-Driven Scene Composition
Scene composition employs a "task-core first" strategy. Task-essential objects (e.g., a cup and a table) derived from instructions are placed first and their coordinates are frozen. Surrounding walls and room elements are then constructed around them using Infinigen. This prevents randomized environment generation from invalidating task feasibility.

It illustrates 3D generation from text and images along with the VLM multi-view QA loop (L0–L2), part segmentation, convex decomposition, and physical property estimation (L3–L4), followed by simulation verification and export to simulator formats (URDF/MJCF/USD) at L5.
captions.F3: The task-driven scene composition procedure. A "task core" consisting of target objects and supporting surfaces is first assembled from task instructions and frozen in place, around which room walls and peripheral furniture are populated to generate diverse room environments while guaranteeing task feasibility.
captions.F4: Examples of task-aligned scenes generated from text instructions. Diverse room layouts and arrangements of furniture and props—such as picking up an item from a desk or retrieving a spice jar from a kitchen counter—are seamlessly composed according to instructions without conflicts.

sections.heading: From Physical Behavior Consistency to Policy Learning and Real-Robot Validation
sections.summary: Using RFW-R assets, the authors evaluated physical property annotation accuracy, behavioral consistency across four physics simulators, grasp success rates across six hands, scene fulfillment rates, and policy learning performance on RoboTwin. RFW-R outperformed major existing datasets across all evaluations.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Asset Annotation and Physical Representation Consistency
In VLM-based part-level semantic evaluations, RFW-R achieved a category consistency of 0.981 and functional consistency of 0.860, scoring highest among comparisons (including EmbodiedGen v2 and PhysX-3D). Numerical validation across 2,424 assets showed that mass discrepancies after exporting to URDF/MJCF were bounded within $1.5 \times 10^{-6}$, and the relative error between summed part masses and holistic mass was within $10^{-3}$ for 98.5% of assets. Compared to "solid fill" (which assumes uniform density), RFW-R's native representation with part-specific densities achieved roughly 7.5 to 9.2 percentage points higher pass rates in drop tests, demonstrating the importance of accurately modeling shifts in center of mass and inertia.

### 4.2 Cross-Simulator Drop Response Consistency
Identical assets (2,257 objects) were imported into four representative engines—PyBullet, MuJoCo, Genesis, and Isaac Sim—and dropped freely from three heights and five orientations to measure displacement, rotation, and penetration. The cross-engine pass consistency reached 80.77% (Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.481$), with MuJoCo and Genesis achieving 94.20% agreement (correlation $r = 0.919$). This confirms that RFW-R's physical representations function universally without engine dependence.

### 4.3 Multi-Fingered Grasp Execution
Grasp execution tests were conducted in the Genesis simulator using six robotic hands (including Ability, Inspire, and Shadow) based on annotated grasps. Exploring up to 64 candidates yielded a macro-average lift success rate of 79.5% and a perturbed robust grasp success rate of 73.7% across all hands. While Ability and Inspire hands achieved high success rates exceeding 90%, the Shadow hand saw lower success due to high degrees of freedom and delicate control requirements, highlighting realistic behavioral differences across hand morphologies.

### 4.4 Policy Learning and Real-Robot Trajectory Replay
Across five RoboTwin benchmark tasks, 100 demonstration episodes per task were collected for each asset source to train Diffusion Policy-based $\pi_{0.5}$ models under identical conditions. In clean environments, policies trained on RFW-R achieved a macro success rate of 71.2%, exceeding the strongest baseline, ManiTwin (55.4%), by 15.8 percentage points. Under randomized settings varying appearance and table heights, it maintained 41.8%, retaining a 10.6 percentage point advantage over the baseline (31.2%). Furthermore, retargeting simulation-generated end-effector trajectories onto a real Piper robot verified successful pick-and-place execution on physical objects across all five tasks.

### 4.5 Scene Composition and Fulfillment
Scene fulfillment was evaluated across 16 fixed room floor plans against furniture and prop placement requests (265 instances across 153 groups). While ManiTwin fulfilled 240 instances and EmbodiedGen v2 fulfilled 258, RFW-R successfully placed all 265 requests (100%). It also ranked highest in VLM-evaluated scene aesthetics and arrangement quality, scoring 3.878 out of 10.

captions.F6: Experimental results of replaying simulation-learned trajectories on a physical robot (Piper). Across five tasks, Grasp, Lift, and Place phases are shown executing consistently between simulation and the real robot.

sections.heading: Toward a Standard Physical Infrastructure for Embodied AI
sections.summary: RFW-W unites over one million diverse physical assets with task-driven scene generation, establishing a simulation learning foundation capable of withstanding real-world complexity. This infrastructure marks a solid step forward for scaling robot learning.
sections.details:
This study presented RFW-W, a million-scale physical asset universe encompassing rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Focusing on the rigid collection RFW-R, the authors demonstrated the efficacy of category-guided generation, multi-stage VLM quality assurance, part-level physical property estimation, and simulation-verified multi-fingered grasp annotations.

Leveraging RFW-R assets enabled 100% request fulfillment in instruction-conditioned scene composition and significantly enhanced manipulation policy learning success rates. This marks a paradigm shift from mere "visual 3D datasets" to "physically executable interaction environments." Future work is expected to expand grasp and affordance annotations for articulated and deformable objects and move toward dynamic world generation.

sections.heading: Appendix: Data Distribution, Physical Assignment Details, and Diagnostic Protocols
sections.summary: The appendix details asset category distributions, part-level mass and density allocation mechanisms, geometric repair criteria, and comprehensive protocols for cross-simulator drop test evaluations.
sections.details:
### Asset Distribution and Deduplication Screening
RFW-R spans 30 domains and 1,212 categories, with an effective coverage (entropy-equivalent category count) of 905.1, demonstrating overwhelming breadth compared to existing datasets skewed toward specific categories (e.g., 7.8 in PhysX-3D). In a 2,424-asset subset sampling two objects per category, image feature-based deduplication revealed that suspected near-duplicate clusters accounted for only 2.27%, confirming high intra-category diversity.

### Part-Level Physical Assignment vs. Solid Fill
Taking a frying pan or a hammer as an example, the density of a frying pan's metal base differs substantially from its wooden or plastic handle. In RFW-R, distinct densities $\rho_p$ are assigned per part and mass is integrated from volume $V_p$, bringing the center of mass and rotational inertia much closer to real tools. In contrast, assuming uniform density across the entire object shifts the center of mass of a hammer—which should be head-heavy—toward the handle, causing its simulated behavior during lifting or swinging to deviate from reality.

### Geometric Diagnostics and Drop Test Thresholds
To ensure collision geometry quality, checks are enforced for connected component counts, boundary edge ratios, and solidity (volume ratio relative to the convex hull). In drop response tests from heights of 0.05m, 0.15m, and 0.30m, stability is strictly evaluated against thresholds requiring horizontal displacement $\le \max(0.05\,\mathrm{m}, 0.1d)$ (where $d$ is object bounding diameter), orientation change $\le 8^\circ$, and floor penetration $< 0.01\,\mathrm{m}$.

captions.F9: Visualization of part-level physical property allocation. For a frying pan and a hammer, volume-proportional uniform density allocation (gray) is compared against RFW-R's allocation based on estimated material densities (blue). Realistic mass distributions are preserved for tools where head and handle densities differ significantly.

takeaways: Robot learning crucially requires shifting from appearance-only 3D generative models to "physically executable assets" complete with collision geometry, mass distribution, friction, and grasp poses.
Part-level material and density estimation more accurately reproduces centers of mass and inertia compared to uniform density (solid fill), improving behavioral stability in simulation.
Fixing task-essential objects (the task core) within the simulation before populating the surrounding room reconciles environmental diversity with task feasibility.
Collecting demonstrations from a physically consistent, high-quality asset library significantly improves downstream manipulation policy success rates using the same number of demonstration episodes.
limitations: Detailed evaluations and downstream policy learning experiments in this paper are primarily focused on rigid bodies (RFW-R); learning complex interactions involving articulated (RFW-A) and deformable (RFW-S) objects remains future work.
Real-robot validation was limited to open-loop replay of simulation trajectories, without running closed-loop policy inference on live real-world camera observations.
Certain assets with thin openings or complex geometries struggle to maintain watertight meshes, restricting volume-based precise evaluation to a subset of assets.
